## Paper

## Abstract

Optical spectrometers are indispensable tools across various fields, from chemical and biological sensing to astronomical observations and quantum technologies. However, the integration of spectrometers onto photonic chips has been hindered by the low spectral resolution or large device footprint with complex multiple channel operations. Here, we introduce a chip-integrated spectrometer by leveraging the acoustically-stimulated Brillouin scattering in a hybrid photonic-phononic chip. The Brillouin interaction provides a dynamic reflection grating with a high reflectivity up to 50% and a fast switching time on the microsecond scale, achieving a spectral resolution of 0.56 nm over a 110 nm bandwidth using just a single 1 mm-long straight waveguide. This performance approaches the fundamental limit of resolution for a given device size, validating the potential of the hybrid photonic-phononic device for efficient and dynamically-reconfigurable spectral analysis, and thus opens up the avenues for advanced optical signal processing and sensing applications.

---

## Introduction

Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) have emerged as a powerful platform1–6, which has the potential to revolutionize the way we generate, process, and manipulate light. By integrating various optical components onto a single chip, PICs enable the realization of sophisticated optical systems that offer unparalleled scalability, low power consumption, high stability, and enhanced light-matter interaction. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of PIC technologies, leading to notable achievements in various fields, such as ultra-high data transmission rates in optical communications7, ultra-sensitive biosensors8, and quantum photonic devices for secure communication and computation9. To further unlock the capability of PIC in spectroscopic analysis for astronomy measurements10,11, medical diagnostics12, environmental monitoring13, and chemical analysis14,15, high-performance optical spectrometers are indispensable16–18.

However, the full integration of spectrometers onto photonic chips faces a fundamental trade-off between spectral resolving capability and device footprint16. Conventional spectrometers mostly rely on static dispersive elements, which could be directly extended to PICs19–21. For example, the grating shown in Fig. 1a separates light of different colors into distinct channels. While the grating offers a wide detection wavelength range, achieving high spectral resolution necessitates a large device length and a dense array of collection channels. The spectral resolution of a grating-based spectrometer is approximately given by Δ λ=λ2=n_eff L sinθ_1 + sinθ_2, where L is the grating length, n_eff is the effective refractive index of the guided optical mode, λ is the light wavelength, and θ is the angle between the input (output) optical beam and the grating. An alternative approach is to employ dynamically tunable dispersive devices, such as Mach-Zehnder interferometers22–24 shown in Fig. 1b. These devices offer potential advantages including higher optical throughput, reduced device footprint, and requirement of fewer detection channels. Nonetheless, the resolution of this approach is limited by the device’s tuning capability. The spectral resolution of a tunable interferometer-based spectrometer is given by Δ λ=λ2/n_eff ΔL with ΔL is the tuning path difference of the interferometer. The requirement for a large tuning length δnΔL ≫ λ, where δn is the variation of the material refractive index. This requirement imposes a practical limitation of the spectrometer size L, limiting it to the order of centimeters, even with the enhancement provided by microrings25. Consequently, there is a pressing need for an approach that combines the advantages of both static and dynamic dispersive elements, enabling the realization of compact, single-channel on-chip spectrometers.

Here, we introduce a fundamentally different approach to integrated spectroscopy that leverages acoustically-stimulated backward Brillouin scattering, a nonlinear optical interaction between photons and acoustic phonons in a medium (Fig. 1c). By harnessing the strong interaction between guided optical and acoustic modes in a carefully engineered lithium niobate (LN) waveguide, we demonstrate a high-resolution, compact, and fully integrated spectrometer with an intrinsic spectral resolution of 0.56 nm over a wavelength range exceeding 110 nm, while maintaining a compact footprint of just 1 mm in length. Our approach provides a coherent interface between the optical spectrometer and radio frequency (RF) control, allowing fast spectral sweeping, with a typical sweep duration of 0.1 seconds and could potentially be even faster. Furthermore, our demonstration of a hybrid photonic-phononic circuit can be extended to incorporate other photonic, electronic, and phononic devices on a single chip, paving the way for fully integrated and multi-functional spectroscopic systems and also for a wide range of photonic-phononic hybrid devices.

---

## Results

Figure 1 illustrates the conceptual schematics of conventional integrated spectrometers and the principle of the proposed approach based on Brillouin scattering9,26–29. Traditional on-chip spectrometers typically rely on linear optical processes, such as dispersive elements in Fig. 1a or Fourier-transform techniques in Fig. 1b. In contrast, our spectrometer exploits the nonlinear Brillouin interaction between guided photonic and phononic modes in a compact waveguide platform (Fig. 1c)30. At the heart of our device is a straight waveguide that supports both optical and acoustic modes, which are coupled primarily through the photoelastic effect. The waveguide is integrated with a compact interdigital transducer (IDT) for RF-to-acoustic wave conversion and with grating couplers that enable efficient excitation and detection of the optical response. When operating the spectrometer, an input optical signal (ω_1) is coupled into the waveguide and interacts with a counter-propagating acoustic wave (Ω) generated by the IDT.

The Brillouin scattering process manifests as a coherent three-wave mixing (TWM) interaction, leading to a wavelength-dependent coupling between forward and backward optical signals stimulated by acoustic wave fields. This coherent TWM results in a frequency-shifted output signal (ω_2) that satisfies both the energy and momentum conservation conditions: ω_2 = ω_1 + Ω and k_2 = k_1 + β, where k and β are the wave vectors of the input (output) optical signal and acoustic wave, respectively. In a simpler picture, the acoustic wave modulates the refractive index along the waveguide through the photoelastic effect, and thus the waveguide can be understood as a dynamic optical grating. Therefore, our spectrometer resembles a linear grating spectrometer (Fig. 1a) with the corresponding input and output angles θ_1 = θ_2 = π/2, allowing us to achieve a spectral resolution approaching the theoretical upper bound of λ2/2n_eff L for a given interaction length L. Moreover, our single-channel device can resolve a wide spectral range through dynamically reconfigurable β by simply sweeping the external RF drive frequency.

To experimentally validate our ultra-compact spectrometer, we fabricate the hybrid phononic and photonic circuits using thin-film LN on sapphire substrate. The combination single-crystal LN and sapphire allows for low-loss photonic and phononic waveguides, while LN’s strong piezoelectric and photoelastic properties facilitate efficient interfacing among the RF, acoustic, and optical signals, making it an ideal material platform for our spectrometer. The device, shown in Fig. 2b, features a straight waveguide with a width of 1.2 μm, a thickness of 400 nm, and a wedge step of 180 nm. This carefully designed geometry supports both optical modes at telecom wavelengths and acoustic modes around 8.5 GHz, with a phase-matched phonon wavelength of 400 nm. The corresponding mode profiles of the photonic and phononic modes are shown in Fig. 2d and g. To excite and focus the acoustic wave into the waveguide, we employ a fan-shaped IDT (Fig. 2c) driven by a RF signal from a vector network analyzer (VNA). The RF S11 parameter of the transducer, as shown in Fig. 2f, exhibits a resonance frequency of 8.5 GHz, indicating the efficient generation of high-frequency guided phonons into the waveguide.

To efficiently couple phonons and photons into the same waveguide for Brillouin interaction, while protecting the electrodes from potential damage caused by direct interaction between the input laser and the IDT, we have designed a hybrid phononic-photonic multiplexing device, as shown in Fig. 2e. This device exploits the tighter confinement of the phononic mode, allowing it to propagate through the waveguide with minimal coupling to adjacent waveguide due to the weak evanescent acoustic field. In contrast, the photonic mode can be efficiently transferred between the two waveguides when passing through the coupling region. Optical input and output couplings are achieved using grating couplers for high signal-to-noise ratio or using side couplings to avoid the sensitivity of coupling efficiency to wavelength and achieve a large wavelength bandwidth couple (A more detailed discussion provided in the Supplementary Information II.)

The experimental setup for characterizing the Brillouin scattering is depicted in Fig. 2a. A tunable laser, amplified by an erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) and with its polarization controlled, is coupled into the waveguide. The reflected optical signal at the selected wavelength, which satisfies the phase-matching condition of Brillouin scattering in the spectrometer, is collected and directed to a photodetector. To investigate the spectrometer’s performance, we fixed the input optical wavelength at 1576 nm and scanned the input RF signal supplied by the VNA, measuring the reflected light intensity with an interaction length L = 1 mm. The result, shown in Fig. 2h, demonstrates the remarkably reflection of the acoustically-induced dynamic grating. The spectrum exhibits a narrow linewidth, with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of just 3.4 MHz, validating the highly selective spectral response and also sub-μs switching time for high-resolution on-chip spectral analysis. Moreover, with an RF drive power of only 20 mW, as shown in Fig. 3a, the grating achieves a peak reflectivity of 50%, which highlights the efficient Brillouin interaction enabled by the carefully engineered hybrid photonic-phononic waveguide.

Figure 3 demonstrates the broadband performance of our spectrometer. In Fig. 3a, the responses for monochromatic optical input signals are measured for different wavelengths ranging from 1514 to 1624 nm, with an experimental wavelength of 110 nm limited by the spectral range of our testing optical source. The linear dependence between the input and reflected optical powers, as shown in the left inset of Fig. 3a, verifies the coherent TWM process of acoustically-stimulated Brillouin scattering. The right inset of Fig. 3a depicts the linear dispersion relationship between the frequency shift of the output light and the input optical wavelength, with a slope of 6.03 MHz/nm. Combined with the narrow bandwidth of the RF response [Fig. 2h], we derive an optical intrinsic spectral resolution of 0.56 nm. The envelope of the varying peak values represent the frequency-dependent RF-phonon conversion efficiency, which is determined by the bandwidth of the IDT. It is worth noting that the observed fluctuations on this envelope reflect the complete, wavelength-dependent system transfer function, which includes not only the IDT response but also factors such as the intrinsic acousto-optic coupling strength and on-chip polarization effects. This entire repeatable response is captured in the calibration matrix used for spectral reconstruction. Although the experimental data is acquired over a 110 nm range, our analysis (Supplementary Information) indicates that the spectrometer can operate over a significantly broader wavelength range. Based on the characteristics of the current IDT design, we estimate that the dynamic range of the spectrometer exceeds 150 nm. Furthermore, by employing advanced broadband IDT designs or cascaded IDTs on a single waveguide, the operating range can potentially be extended to 300 nm or more.

To directly demonstrate the sub-nanometer resolution of our spectrometer, we perform a spectral measurement using a source consisting of two laser tones as input, with a wavelength interval of only 0.5 nm. By scanning the RF drive frequency, we obtain the spectral information shown in Fig. 3b. The raw data clearly show two distinctly resolved peaks. We fit the data using a double-Lorentzian function, which is the sum of two Lorentzian distributions displayed in red. Furthermore, by using the spectral response for monochromatic light in Fig. 3a, we reconstruct the input spectrum with respect to the optical wavelength. The retrieved wavelength data are consistent with our input laser wavelengths, proving that the projected resolution of our spectrometer can be much better than 0.5 nm.

To further demonstrate the fluorescence measurement capability of our spectrometer and its potential in telecom applications, we use an EDFA to generate a broadband spectrum and utilize a dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) filter to synthesize a broadband light source. The DWDM filter allows us to selectively switch on and off specific bandpass channels (e.g., C23-C26) to create controlled spectral features. As shown in Fig. 3c, the spectrum is first measured using a commercial spectrometer as a reference. In our device, the input signal from our device is directly detected by a PD. The response spectrum in Fig. 3c (blue line) reveals a frequency-independent background noise floor, which we attribute to reflections of the input signal in our system, primarily due to the backward scattering from the coupler. By mapping the RF response to the optical domain, we derive the optical spectrum, which exhibit excellent agreement with the reference spectrum measured by a commercial spectrometer (orange line). This measurement result demonstrates that our spectrometer possesses the capability to resolve fluorescence spectra and is well-suited for DWDM, which is widely used in the telecom technology.

In Fig. 4a, we compare the performance of our device with state-of-the-art demonstrations reported in the literature19–23,25,31–35, focusing on the intrinsic spectral resolution of the devices. The intrinsic spectral resolution is governed by the dispersive path of the device, which is determined by its inherent optical response bandwidth, regardless of the input signal strength, detection noises, and the reconstruction algorithms36–40. Our device exhibits high performance in terms of resolution and footprint. According to the coherent mode conversion in an ideal uniform waveguide, the intrinsic resolution is determined by the phase-matching condition in the coupled mode equations41 (Supplementary Information). For a fixed RF frequency, the reflected light has a bandwidth corresponding to the FWHM of the wave vector Δ β ≈ 5.56/L, which implies a fundamental trade-off relation between resolution and footprint. Considering the dispersion relation of the photonic mode as ∂β/∂λ = 1.2 × 10^4 rad/(m · nm), the fundamental limitation of resolution is given by Δ λ = Δ β / (∂β/∂λ) = 460 / L μm nm: (1)

For an interaction length L = 1 mm in our device, the resolution limit for an ideal lossless waveguide is 0.46 nm, indicating that our experimental result of 0.56 nm approaches this fundamental limit with a small discrepancy attributed to the losses. Also, we find that the practical resolution of our spectrometer does not improve with further increases in L, revealing the constraints imposed by the propagation loss of the phononic mode in the waveguide. As shown by the red lines in Fig. 4b, the resolution considering the phonon attenuation is calculated for given equivalent phononic quality factors (Q), and a phonon Q ~ 3000 explains our observations of the saturated resolution for L > 1 mm. Furthermore, the potential imperfections of non-uniform waveguide cross-section can introduce variations in the mode wave vectors, which can be treated as a phase-matching diffusion process in the mode conversion and reduce the resolution. The dependence of the phase mismatching Δβ on the variation of the waveguide width (Δw) and film thickness (Δt) is shown in Fig. 4c, demonstrating that the two geometry parameters independently contribute to the mismatching. By assuming a random walk of Δβ and the accumulated mismatch in the interaction region following a normal distribution, we numerically simulate the influence of the phase-matching diffusion with a standard deviation σ = 1500 rad/m for different phonon Q (Supplementary Information). The results are plotted in Fig. 4b as dots, with the shaded area representing the standard deviation. These results show that the impact of phase-matching diffusion becomes more pronounced for higher Q. Therefore, a resolution of 0.1 nm with an interaction length under 6 mm is feasible by improving phonon Q by one order of magnitude42 and suppressing the variation of Δβ through compensating for film thickness variations via specially designed modulations in the waveguide width43.

---

## Methods

Device fabrication process
We fabricate the hybrid phononic and photonic circuits using LN-on-sapphire structure. In this work, we use x-cut LN-on-sapphire wafer featuring 400 nm LN layer on a 400 μm thick sapphire substrate. The fabrication process of the LN-on-sapphire chip involves two main steps. First, we define the optical waveguides using hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) as the resist using electron beam lithography (EBL). The structures are then etched using argon etching. The optical wedge waveguides are formed by partially etching the LN layer by 220 nm, leaving a 180 nm-thick slab layer. Second, an interdigital transducer (IDT) structure are defined in another EBL step using polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) resist. A layer of 20 nm Aluminum is then deposited on the top of LN using an electron beam evaporator, followed by a liftoff process.

Spectrometer characterizing
In our experiment, we designed different optical coupling structures and testing setups for various application scenarios. Regarding optical coupling, we utilized different coupling methods. We employed both grating coupling and side coupling to achieve efficient input-output relationships. Meanwhile, we implemented two distinct testing methods: one is the heterodyne detection method mentioned in Fig. 2(a), and the other directly measures the intensity of the reflected signal via a photodiode shown in Fig. 3c. Side coupling is typically combined with heterodyne detection due to its advantage in enabling broadband signal measurement without the coupling efficiency being affected by wavelength. However, side coupling tends to introduce significant background reflection noise, which can lower the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) when directly reading the reflected signal power. To address this, heterodyne detection is employed to enhance the SNR, as demonstrated by the data in Fig. 3a.

Data availability
All data generated or analysed during this study are available within the paper and its Supplementary Information. Further source data will be made available on request.

Code availability
The code used to solve the equations presented in the Supplementary Information will be made available on request.

tool or home-grown software?.
Response: Thank you for your question. The term 'quasi-Love' mode, mentioned in the caption
of Figure 2, describes the specific acoustic modes in our waveguide. A classical Love wave is
a guided acoustic wave where the particle motion is purely an in-plane (horizontal) shear
displacement. In our acoustic waveguide, the 'quasi-Love' mode is an acoustic mode
characterized by predominantly horizontal vibration. Further, this 'quasi-Love' mode is ideal
for our application because its strong in-plane shear component couples very efficiently to the
optical TE mode via lithium niobate's photoelastic tensor, and is easy to excite via IDT, leading
to the strong Brillouin interaction we utilize. For a more comprehensive theoretical treatment
of such guided acoustic waves in thin films, we refer to Wang et al. (W. Wang, M. Shen, C.-L.
Zou, W. Fu, Z. Shen, and H. X. Tang, High-Acoustic-Index-Contrast Phononic Circuits:
Numerical Modeling, J. Appl. Phys. 128, (2020)), which we now cite as Ref [30] in the main
text.
Regarding the numerical modeling, all numerical results of the optical and acoustic modes, such
as the mode profiles shown in Figures 2c and 2g, were performed using the finite element
method with the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics. To clarify this point, we have
added a sentence in the caption of Fig. 2 as:
“Displacement and electric field distributions at the waveguide cross-section for the quasi-
Love phononic mode and the fundamental transverse electric photonic mode, respectively.
All these simulations were performed using the finite element method (COMSOL
Multiphysics).”
Comment 3: I also wondered about the suggestion of a potential elastic Q of 20000. What is
the upper limit to this imposed by viscosity?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment. The potential acoustic Q-factor
of 20,000 proposed in our paper is based on the experimental results reported in Ref. [42] (I. L.
Bajak, A. McNab, J. Richter, and C. D. W. Wilkinson, Attenuation of Acoustic Waves in Lithium
Niobate, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 69, 689 (1981)). According to the measurement in bulk lithium
niobate, we estimate the corresponding quality factor for bulk lithium niobate at a frequency of
8.5 GHz. This value represents a lower bound of the achievable acoustic quality factor that
limited by the material absorption.
The discrepancy between this potential value and the Q-factor of ~3000 measured in our device
strongly indicates that our current performance is limited by extrinsic loss mechanisms
introduced during fabrication, rather than by the material absorption itself. These extrinsic
losses arise from two primary sources:
1) The imperfections arising from the wafer production process. The commercial LN-on-
sapphire films are typically produced via an ion-slicing method, which is known to
introduce residual lattice damage that acts as a scattering center for phonons.
2) The surface scattering from the etched imperfect sidewalls of the waveguide. Because our
phononic mode is tightly confined, it interacts strongly with these surfaces, meaning any
fabrication-induced roughness causes significant phononic scattering loss.
Considering these factors, performance improvements can be achieved by optimizing
nanofabrication processes to minimize the surface scattering-related losses. Furthermore, to
reach the ultimate quality factor constrained by the intrinsic properties of the materials, future
developments in thin-film material preparation are needed, such as advancements in wafer
bonding techniques and defect repair technologies. We add a paragraph in Supplement VI part
to discussing this as following:
“In addition to expanding the working bandwidth, further improvements lie in enhancing the
intrinsic resolution of the spectrometer by increasing the phonon quality factor. Current devices
exhibit a Q-factor of approximately 3000. We believe this value is not constrained by the
intrinsic acoustic properties of single-crystal lithium niobate but rather by external loss
mechanisms. The significant difference between the experimentally measured quality factor and
the higher Q value derived from bulk material studies indicates substantial room for
improvement. These external losses primarily arise from two sources: inherent defects in the
thin-film wafers and defects introduced during the nanofabrication process.
Therefore, future performance enhancements can be realized through two approaches:
systematically optimizing nanofabrication processes to reduce surface scattering losses, and
further improving the thin-film material preparation techniques, such as enhancing wafer
bonding processes and developing defect repair or annealing technologies suitable for this
material system. Successfully addressing these challenges will pave the way for the emergence
of a new generation of ultra-high-resolution chip-scale Brillouin spectrometers.”

the higher Q value derived from bulk material studies indicates substantial room for

thin-film wafers and defects introduced during the nanofabrication process.
Therefore, future performance enhancements can be realized through two approaches:
systematically optimizing nanofabrication processes to reduce surface scattering losses, and

Comment 3: The platform is Zhengfu architecture–LN on Sapphire. The authors did not
explain why they use this specific combination. One trivial question would be whether
conventional thin film LN on SiO2/Si can be used for this application. If it works, the authors
explain why they use this architecture. If not, the authors explain why the conventional platform
is not working.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. The choice of substrate is a critical design
decision for our hybrid photonic-phononic platform, and we are pleased to have this opportunity
to clarify the reasons behind it. The Zhengfu architecture has three main advantages: (1) tight
optical and acoustic wave confinement in phononic waveguide, (2) low acoustic and optical
losses in single-crystal materials, and (3) the piezoelectricity of the LN material to enable the
efficient conversion between microwave and acoustic wave. These advantages make this
architecture being an idea platform for realizing the hybrid electric-phononic-photonic devices
for advanced applications.
For the potential candidate of the substrate, i.e., the traditional thin-film lithium niobate
architecture based on silicon dioxide (SiO₂)/Si platforms mentioned by the Reviewer, the SiO₂
layer has significant acoustic loss. The performance of our spectrometer relies on the efficient
generation and low-loss propagation of high-frequency (~8.5 GHz) acoustic waves (phonons).
The SiO₂ buried oxide layer in standard LNOI wafers is an amorphous material exhibiting
extremely high acoustic attenuation at the GHz frequencies we utilize. Any acoustic leakage
from the LNOI waveguide into the SiO₂ layer will result in a drastically reduced phonon
lifetime. In contrast, sapphire exhibits inherently low acoustic loss as a single-crystal material.
As discussed in above Reponses, a high phonon Q-factors is critical for achieving high spectral
resolution.
Comment 4: It is clear the device can measure the spectrum of input lights. However, I am
not convinced on the accuracy of light intensity measurement. At a single wavelength, the
reflected optical power has a linear relation (in log-scale) with input power. The linear
coefficients at different wavelengths are the function of the frequency-dependent RF-phonon
conversion efficiency, which is determined by the bandwidth of the IDT (yellow shaded area in
Fig3-a). However, I found that the reflected light powers are not following the conversion
efficiency curve. In this situation, it would be very difficult to guess the power of input light at
different wavelengths.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this sharp observation. The reviewer is correct that the
measured reflection peak in Figure 3a (the figure below) does not perfectly align with the
idealized IDT efficiency envelope. However, this deviation does not represent a measurement
error. Actually, we have repeated the measurement many times, and the results are reproducible.
Therefore, the stable response of the spectrometer at different microwave frequency indicates
that standard calibration procedures must be performed on the system.
The reasons for the observed bandwidth difference lie in the fact that the final optical reflected
power results from the combined effects of multiple wavelength-dependent mechanisms, not
solely the electro-acoustic conversion response of the IDT. Key influencing factors include:
1) Wavelength-dependent Acousto-Optic Coupling: The intrinsic coupling strength of the
Brillouin interaction itself varies with the optical wavelength, directly affecting the
reflection efficiency.
2) Photonic Multiplexer Response: The on-chip phononic-photonic multiplexing device,
which acts as a directional coupler to guide light into the interaction region, has a
wavelength-sensitive transfer efficiency.
3) Polarization-Dependent Coupling: The system exhibits high sensitivity to input
polarization state, primarily due to two factors: First, the Brillouin interaction is
specifically designed for the fundamental TE mode; Second, the grating couplers used
for input/output exhibit both polarization-dependent and wavelength-dependent
response characteristics. Light output from standard input fibers cannot maintain a
constant polarization state across the entire spectrum. Despite manual optimization of
coupling using a polarization controller, residual fluctuations cause the optical power
injected into the target chip's TE mode to vary with wavelength. This directly results
in fluctuations in the system transfer function. In practical applications, this issue can
be addressed by employing a fully polarization-maintaining optical path.
The key point is that this complex transfer function, arising from the combination of all these
effects, is stable and repeatable. The data in Figure 3a is therefore not a flaw, but rather the
essential dataset used for calibration. As described in the Supplementary Information (Section
IV), we use this data to construct a calibration matrix M that empirically captures the complete
system response. Accurate intensity measurements of an unknown source are then achieved by
measuring its raw output and mathematically applying this calibration matrix to retrieve the
true input spectrum. The high agreement with commercial spectrometers shown in Figure 3c
(the figure below) strongly demonstrates that this standard calibration procedure enables the
device to perform precise intensity measurements across its operational bandwidth.
To clarify this point, we add a sentence in the main text in page 5:
“Figure3 demonstrates the broadband performance of our spectrometer……. It is worth noting
that the observed fluctuations on this envelope reflect the complete, wavelength-dependent
system transfer function, which includes not only the IDT response but also factors such as the
intrinsic acousto-optic coupling strength and on-chip polarization effects. This entire
repeatable response is captured in the calibration matrix used for spectral reconstruction.”
Response to Reviewer #3
General comment: The manuscript titled “Compact and high-resolution spectrometer via
Brillouin integrated circuits” demonstrates a waveguide-based device integrated with
interdigital transducer to excite acoustic waves which then scatter the input optical signal. The
study proposes its use as a compact spectrometer.
Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #3 for the careful reading of our manuscript and for
raising important questions regarding the fundamental operating principle and novelty of our
work. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify these critical distinctions.
We note that the other expert reviewers have recognized the fundamental novelty and
significance of our approach. Reviewer #1 specifically stated: “As far as I can tell, this is the
first demonstration of IDT-induced on-chip Brillouin scattering for spectroscopy” and
concluded that “this technology could have significant commercial impact for compact
precision optical spectroscopy.” and that the work “could warrant publication in Nature
Communications.” Similarly, Reviewer #2 acknowledged that “the principle of spectrometer is
rather simple, coming from the linear relationship between Brillouin shifts and pump
wavelengths” and concluded the paper “could be quite interesting to relevant community.”
These assessments reflect recognition of our key innovation: we demonstrate the first chip-
scale spectrometer based on electronically-controlled acoustic pumping of Brillouin scattering,
fundamentally distinct from all prior Brillouin-based optical systems.
In the following, we address the comments raised by Reviewer #3 one-by-one:
Comment 1: I do not see it any different from a pump-probe Brillouin scattering experiment
in an integrated waveguide, where tuning the pump wavelength results in tuning of the Stokes
frequency at which maximum gain would occur.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the Reviewer’s comments. We believe there is a
fundamental misunderstanding of the working principle of our device, which is distinct from a
conventional pump-probe stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) experiment. Just as the other
two expert reviewers pointed out this crucial distinction in their comments:
 Reviewer #1 accurately described our method, noting, "the GHz acoustic wave is
generated by an on-chip IDT device directed into the waveguide" and concluded that this
is "the first demonstration of IDT-induced on-chip Brillouin scattering for spectroscopy."
 Reviewer #2 correctly highlighted the use of an "external IDT on LiNbO3 at around
8.5GHz."
The core innovation of our work is that our device operates as an acoustically-pumped
spectrometer. Unlike conventional pump-probe Brillouin experiments that require a strong,
known optical pump laser to mediate the interaction, our method requires no optical pump
whatsoever. The only optical input is the unknown signal to be measured. The role of the
"pump" is fulfilled by a tunable, electronically-generated acoustic wave, which stimulates the
reflection of the input signal. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a spectrometer
based on this purely acoustically-driven principle.
Furthermore, our device specifically leverages backward Brillouin scattering, a configuration
which maximizes the photoacoustic interaction and allows the spectrometer's resolution to
approach the fundamental limit for a given device length, as explained in the manuscript. This
unique combination of acoustic drive mechanisms with high-resolution backscattering
geometry is the core feature of our work.
Comment 2: Further, the input power of the optical signal has to be above a few hundreds
microwatts for the device to generate a detectable backscattered signal with good signal-to-
noise ratio, which places a minimum threshold on the power of the optical signal to be detected.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this issue. We would like to clarify that the device
operates at lower power levels than suggested. The inset of Figure 3a in the main manuscript
(as shown in the figure below) explicitly demonstrates that the linear relationship between input
and reflected power holds down to the lowest measured input power of 100 µW. The reflect
ratio shown in Figure 3a indicates that over 50% input signal can be reflected and then
measured by our detector using direct photodetection or heterodyne detection scheme. So the
limitation of our device signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) arises from imperfections in the detection
module and the optical coupling interfaces, rather than from the Brillouin process itself. The
SNR for measuring even weaker signals can be further enhanced by increasing the scanning
time or the number of averages.
Comment 3: Further, it will be better to compare the input spectrum using the both commercial
spectrometer and the proposed device using the same scale (log or linear).
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this nice suggestion. We agree that presenting both
spectra on a common scale would provide a more direct and quantitative comparison. In the
revised version of the manuscript, we have updated Figure 3c, which plot the spectrum data
from both our device and the commercial spectrometer on a normalized linear scale to better
illustrate the high fidelity of our instrument. The updated Figure 3c is shown as below:
Comment 4: The resolution of 0.56 nm achieved in this demonstration is much lower than what
has been obtained using the Brillouin dynamic gratings in optical fiber (Optics Letters Vol. 39,
Issue 10, pp. 2967-2970 (2014)) or photonic chip (Optics Letters Vol. 38, Issue 3, pp. 305-307
(2013)).
Response: Thank you for your comment. We would like to respectfully clarify that a direct
comparison of resolution with the cited works is not appropriate, because our device operates
on a fundamentally different principle and serves a distinct function as a spectrometer.
Regarding the working principle, the devices mentioned by the Reviewer rely on optically
pumped stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS). Such systems require (1) high pump laser power
and (2) a calibrated laser for signal detection. For a device to function as a universal
spectrometer, it is impractical and fundamentally limiting to rely on powerful external
calibrated lasers to measure unknown input signals.
Our acoustically pumped device, in complete contrast, is a self-contained spectrometer that uses
a purely electronic (RF) signal to generate the acoustic grating. This allows it to directly analyze
any compatible input optical signal without needing another optical source, which is the core
characteristic of a true spectrometer. Given this fundamental difference in operational principle
and application scope, we believe that a comparison based on a single performance metric such
as resolution is not meaningful.
Furthermore, spectral resolution is intrinsically related to the interaction length (i.e., footprint)
of the device, as dictated by fundamental physics. The primary contribution of our work lies in
achieving unprecedentedly high resolution within a compact device. As shown in Figure 4a (as
shown below), through a comprehensive comparison with other state-of-the-art integrated
spectrometers, our device sets a new performance benchmark within a millimeter-scale
footprint. We believe this is the most critical metric for evaluating the significance and
breakthrough nature of our research in the field of integrated photonics.
